issues.legal_issue: Prolonged delay in completing a large-scale land acquisition does not by itself require the acquisition to be quashed where the landowners contributed to the delay and the land has been developed or is required for public use, but may warrant additional compensation.
material_facts: The acquisitions were initiated for planned urban development, and awards were made many years after the relevant declarations.
Landowners filed objections and numerous court challenges, and interim stays contributed to the delay.
After an earlier Supreme Court decision resolved challenges to the acquisitions, the authorities still delayed making awards without justification.
Development for public use and third-party interests had arisen in acquired lands; some landowners had retained possession and enjoyed the land.
issues.conclusion: The acquisition proceedings were not quashed for delay. The landowners were instead entitled to additional compensation calculated by reference to the market value on the date of the acquisition notification. The same approach applied even where possession had not been taken.
issues.legal_principle: Applying Ram Chand v. Union of India, and considering Bihar State Housing Board v. Ram Behari Mahato and Ujjain Vikas Pradhikaran v. Raj Kumar Johri, delay attributable in part to landowners and the public-interest consequences of quashing may justify preserving the acquisition while compensating landowners for the authorities' unjustified delay. The Court held that the principle applies even where possession has not been taken, particularly where landowners have continued to enjoy its use and benefits.

rule.if: acquisition_challenge and prolonged_acquisition_delay and landowner_challenges_contributed_to_delay and authorities_delayed_after_challenges_resolved and public_development_or_third_party_interests_exist

predicates.acquisition_challenge: The proceeding challenges a compulsory land acquisition.
predicates.prolonged_acquisition_delay: The acquisition authorities took an unusually long time to complete the acquisition.
predicates.landowner_challenges_contributed_to_dela: The landowners' objections or court challenges contributed to the time taken to complete the acquisition.
predicates.authorities_delayed_after_challenges_res: The authorities failed to proceed promptly after the relevant challenges had been resolved.
predicates.public_development_or_third_party_intere: The acquired land had been developed for public use or third-party interests had arisen in it.

issues.definition: When an acquisition challenge concerns a substantially delayed acquisition, the landowners contributed to the delay, the authorities then delayed after the challenges were resolved, and public development or third-party interests exist, the acquisition is preserved while additional compensation is awarded.

issues.legal_issue: Successive declarations concerning different parcels of land covered by a single acquisition notification are permissible when the validating amendment authorizes them.
material_facts: The acquisition notifications covered large areas of land.
More than one declaration was made in respect of land covered by a notification.
The Land Acquisition (Amendment Validation) Act, 1967 amended the governing provisions to permit declarations at different times for different parcels covered by the same notification.
issues.conclusion: The challenge to successive declarations failed; the validating amendment permitted them.
issues.legal_principle: In State of M.P. v. Vishnu Prasad Sharma, the Court had held that the original scheme did not contemplate successive declarations in the circumstances discussed there. The Land Acquisition (Amendment Validation) Act, 1967 amended Sections 5-A and 6 of the Land Acquisition Act, 1894 to permit declarations from time to time for different parcels covered by one notification, and validated earlier acquisitions. Its validity was upheld in Uday Ram Sharma v. Union of India and reaffirmed in Aflatoon v. Lt. Governor of Delhi.

rule.if: acquisition_challenge and one_acquisition_notification and successive_parcel_declarations and validating_law_authorizes_successive_declarations

predicates.acquisition_challenge: The proceeding challenges a compulsory land acquisition.
predicates.one_acquisition_notification: A single initial notification covered the land in question.
predicates.successive_parcel_declarations: Declarations were made at different times for different parcels covered by that notification.
predicates.validating_law_authorizes_successive_dec: A law applicable to the acquisition authorized declarations at different times for separate parcels covered by one notification.

issues.definition: When one acquisition notification covers the land, declarations are made successively for its parcels, and an applicable validating law authorizes that procedure, the successive declarations are authorized.

issues.legal_issue: The constitutional protection concerning land under personal cultivation within the applicable ceiling does not require compensation to be valued on the date of award or possession for land acquired for planned urban development.
material_facts: The land was acquired for planned development rather than agrarian reform.
Some landowners asserted that their land was personally cultivated and within the applicable ceiling limit.
They argued that compensation should reflect the market value when the award was made or possession was taken rather than when the acquisition notification was published.
issues.conclusion: The acquisition was not invalid on this ground, and the applicable market value was the value on the date of publication of the acquisition notification.
issues.legal_principle: Sections 11(1) and 23(1) of the Land Acquisition Act, 1894 provide for market value by reference to the date of publication of the acquisition notification. The Court held that Article 31-A concerns agrarian reform and does not govern acquisition for planned urban development. It relied on Aflatoon v. Lt. Governor of Delhi, P.V. Mudaliar v. Deputy Collector, Nagpur Improvement Trust v. Vithal Rao, Vajravelu v. Special Deputy Collector, and Ram Chand v. Union of India. The second proviso to Article 31-A requires market-value compensation where it applies, but does not shift the valuation date prescribed by the Act in this acquisition.

rule.if: compensation_challenge and acquisition_for_planned_urban_development and acquisition_not_for_agrarian_reform and compensation_value_claimed_at_award_or_possession

predicates.compensation_challenge: The proceeding challenges the basis or amount of compensation for a compulsory acquisition.
predicates.acquisition_for_planned_urban_developmen: The land was acquired for planned urban development.
predicates.acquisition_not_for_agrarian_reform: The acquisition was not for agrarian reform.
predicates.compensation_value_claimed_at_award_or_p: The landowner seeks valuation by reference to the award or taking of possession rather than the acquisition notification.

issues.definition: When compensation is challenged in an acquisition for planned urban development that is not for agrarian reform, a claim for valuation at the award or possession stage does not displace valuation at the notification stage.

issues.legal_issue: A landowner's notice under the planning law does not end an acquisition where the land is not specifically designated for compulsory acquisition in the relevant plans and acquisition has proceeded under the land acquisition law.
material_facts: The landowners relied on a planning-law notice requiring the government to acquire their land within a specified time.
The land was not specifically particularized as required for compulsory acquisition in a master plan or zonal development plan, and no zonal development plans had been prepared for it.
The acquisition notifications under the Land Acquisition Act had already been issued.
The planning law also provided for acquisition for development under the Land Acquisition Act.
issues.conclusion: The notices did not cause the acquisition proceedings to lapse or release the land from acquisition.
issues.legal_principle: Sections 55(1) and 55(2) of the Delhi Development Act, 1957 apply to land designated for compulsory acquisition in the relevant planning documents; the particular land must be shown to have that designation. The Court also relied on Section 15(1), which permits acquisition for development under the Land Acquisition Act, and held that the planning law did not inhibit such acquisition.

predicates.acquisition_challenge: The proceeding challenges a compulsory land acquisition.
predicates.planning_law_notice_given: The landowner served a notice under a planning law requiring the government to acquire the land.
predicates.land_not_specifically_designated_for_com: The relevant planning documents did not specifically designate the land for compulsory acquisition.
predicates.acquisition_process_already_initiated_un: The government had already initiated acquisition of the land under the general land acquisition law.

issues.definition: When a landowner gives a planning-law acquisition notice but the land is not specifically designated for compulsory acquisition and acquisition has already been initiated under the general acquisition law, the notice does not end the acquisition.

issues.legal_issue: The expiry of a master plan's stated period does not by itself invalidate an acquisition for continuing urban development.
material_facts: The landowners argued that the master plan's stated period had expired before the acquisition proceedings were completed.
The acquisition was for the planned development of a growing city facing continuing population growth and housing needs.
The acquisition involved large areas intended for residential and commercial development.
issues.conclusion: The plan's stated period having elapsed did not render the notifications ineffective or require the acquisition proceedings to be quashed.
issues.legal_principle: The Court treated urban development as a continuing process, with no fixed terminal point for development of a growing city. It also noted that Section 11-A of the Land Acquisition Act, 1894 was introduced to impose a completion time frame and protect landowners from undue loss caused by delay.

predicates.acquisition_challenge: The proceeding challenges a compulsory land acquisition.
predicates.master_plan_period_elapsed: The period stated for the applicable master plan had elapsed before completion of the acquisition.
predicates.urban_development_need_continues: The city continued to face growth and development needs for which the land was acquired.

issues.definition: When a challenged acquisition is for urban development that remains necessary, expiry of the master plan's stated period does not invalidate the acquisition.

issues.legal_issue: A purported withdrawal of land from acquisition is ineffective without a valid government withdrawal and the required published notification, and an ineffective partial release does not invalidate the rest of the acquisition.
material_facts: The landowners relied on communications said to convey withdrawal of certain land from acquisition.
The High Court examined the original government record and found that the Minister had directed that the matter be taken up for denotification, rather than having ordered withdrawal himself.
No notification denotifying the acquisition was published.
The alleged withdrawal concerned only some land covered by the acquisition.
issues.conclusion: The communications did not effect a withdrawal, and the acquisition could not be quashed on that basis. Even an otherwise valid partial release would not invalidate the entire acquisition notification.
issues.legal_principle: Section 48(1) of the Land Acquisition Act, 1894 permits withdrawal only before possession is taken. The Court agreed that the government record disclosed no ministerial withdrawal order and held that a withdrawal must be made effective through the required published notification, having regard to Section 21 of the General Clauses Act. It relied on Chandra Bansi Singh v. State of Bihar, State of Maharashtra v. Uma Shankar Rajabhau, and U.P. Jal Nigam v. Kalra Properties, and held that an ineffective or invalid release of part of the land does not invalidate the entire acquisition notification.

predicates.acquisition_challenge: The proceeding challenges a compulsory land acquisition.
predicates.purported_partial_withdrawal: The government or its officials purported to withdraw some, but not all, of the land from acquisition.
predicates.no_published_denotification: No required public notification formally denotifying the acquisition was published.

issues.definition: When a challenged acquisition is met with a purported partial withdrawal but no formal denotification is published, the acquisition remains effective despite the purported release.

issues.legal_issue: Land reserved for recreational facilities may be acquired as part of planned urban development, and existing structures do not automatically entitle owners to exclusion from a large-area acquisition.
material_facts: Some acquired land was shown as reserved for recreational facilities in the master plan.
The acquisition covered thousands of acres for planned development.
Landowners pointed to structures, schools, businesses, residences, a sports complex, and other development on portions of the land.
The record did not establish that the structures predated the acquisition notification or had the required official approval.
The government stated that it would consider the structures and make decisions concerning them.
issues.conclusion: Recreational land was properly treated as part of planned development, and the asserted structures did not justify quashing the acquisition or automatically excluding those portions. The government was left to consider the structures.
issues.legal_principle: Recreational amenities are part of planned development and the life of a developed society. Relying on State of U.P. v. Pista Devi, the Court held that small portions with structures need not be carved out of a large acquisition for planned urban development, particularly where the structures' timing and authorization were not established. The Court left consideration of the structures to the government's discretion.

predicates.acquisition_challenge: The proceeding challenges a compulsory land acquisition.
predicates.large_area_urban_development_acquisition: A large area of land was acquired for planned urban development.
predicates.land_reserved_for_recreation_or_small_bu: The challenged land includes land reserved for recreational use or small portions on which structures stand.
predicates.structures_not_shown_preexisting_and_aut: The evidence does not establish that the structures existed before the acquisition notification and had the required official authorization.

issues.definition: When a large area is acquired for urban development, recreational land or small built-up portions are included, and the structures are not shown to predate the notification and be authorized, those portions are not automatically excluded.
